explanations.answer: No house for the LORD's Name was built yet
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the text gives. The people were still sacrificing on the high places "…because a house for the Name of the LORD had not yet been built." Solomon, David's son and Israel's king, was still busy building that house, along with his palace and the wall (1 Kings 3:1). Anybody who has waited on a building project knows the feeling.

explanations.answer: The king ordered them to go there
explanations.explanation: The text never says the king ordered anything here. It gives one reason, and it's about a building. The people were sacrificing on the high places because a house for the Name of the LORD had not yet been built. So the missing house is the answer, friend, not a royal command.

Good guess, but priests aren't mentioned in this verse at all. What the text says is that a house for the Name of the LORD had not yet been built. That's the reason given for the sacrificing on the high places. So the missing house is the answer, friend.

Yes, the text says it straight out: "…Solomon loved the LORD and walked in the statutes of his father David…" (1 Kings 3:3). The writer puts that right up front. Then comes a little "except," and we'll get to that. The love is real, and the text says so first.

The text says the opposite. "…Solomon loved the LORD and walked in the statutes of his father David…" (1 Kings 3:3). Solomon is David's son and Israel's king, and the writer puts his love for the LORD right at the start. The "except" that follows is about where he sacrificed, not about whether he loved God.

That's the one. The verse says Solomon walked in his father's statutes, "…except that he sacrificed and burned incense on the high places." So the sacrificing and the incense both happened there. Incense is the word in the verse, friend.

Oil, friend? I get it, oil has a nice shine to it, and I bet it smells better than my burnt batches. But the verse says Solomon "…sacrificed and burned incense on the high places." Oil never makes it into that sentence, and incense is the word that does.

Grain makes sense as something people bring to an altar, but it's not in this verse. The text says Solomon "…sacrificed and burned incense on the high places." Incense is the blank. Next time, the verse is your recipe card.

explanations.answer: Ask and I will give it to you
explanations.explanation: Yes! In the dream at Gibeon, God says, "Ask, and I will give it to you!" (1 Kings 3:5). That's an open door for Solomon, Israel's king. I think I'd have stood there with my mouth open for a full minute. What a way to start a dream.

explanations.answer: Go and tear down the high places
explanations.explanation: Nothing in this dream says that. God's words are, "Ask, and I will give it to you!" (1 Kings 3:5). The high places are mentioned in the verses before, but God doesn't bring them up in the dream. His first words to Solomon are an invitation to ask.

explanations.answer: Rise and lead My people out
explanations.explanation: That's not what God says here. In the dream He tells Solomon, "Ask, and I will give it to you!" (1 Kings 3:5). There's no leading anybody out in this scene. It's a king being told he can ask for something.

Right. Solomon says God showed his father David loving devotion "…because he walked before You in faithfulness, righteousness, and uprightness of heart." (1 Kings 3:6). Notice Solomon honors his dad before he asks for a single thing. That's a good way to start a conversation with God.

Solomon doesn't say anything about birth order. His reason is that David "…walked before You in faithfulness, righteousness, and uprightness of heart." (1 Kings 3:6). It's about how David walked, friend. Nothing about where he stood in line.

explanations.answer: David asked Him for great riches
explanations.explanation: Riches, friend? Solomon doesn't bring up money when he talks about his father. He says God showed David loving devotion "…because he walked before You in faithfulness, righteousness, and uprightness of heart." (1 Kings 3:6). David's faithful walk is what Solomon points to. David never gets a price tag in that sentence.

That's it. Solomon says, "But I am only a little child, not knowing how to go out or come in." (1 Kings 3:7). Here is a king saying he doesn't know how to do the job. I think that kind of honesty takes some nerve.

Shepherd is a fair guess for someone leading people, but it's not the word Solomon uses. He says, "But I am only a little child, not knowing how to go out or come in." (1 Kings 3:7). The word is child. He's describing himself as small, and he says it to God.

Solomon doesn't call himself a soldier. He says, "But I am only a little child, not knowing how to go out or come in." (1 Kings 3:7). The word is child. He's talking about not knowing how to do the job, and nothing about fighting.

Yes. Solomon says he's among the people God chose, "…a people too numerous to count or number." (1 Kings 3:8). That's a lot of people for one king to lead. Count them? Friend, I can't even count the crumbs on my counter.

The text says they are too many to count. Solomon says he's among the people God chose, "…a people too numerous to count or number." (1 Kings 3:8). So the statement is true, friend. I think that's why he sounds so aware of the size of the job.

explanations.answer: A heart to judge with understanding
explanations.explanation: That's exactly what he asks for. "Therefore give Your servant an understanding heart to judge Your people and to discern between good and evil." (1 Kings 3:9). God said ask, and Solomon asked for help doing the job. I think that's one of the best requests ever made.

explanations.answer: Wealth to build a great kingdom
explanations.explanation: Wealth is what many of us would grab, but Solomon doesn't ask for it. He asks for "…an understanding heart to judge Your people and to discern between good and evil." (1 Kings 3:9). God even points out later that Solomon didn't ask for wealth (1 Kings 3:11). Hold onto that, friend, because it matters.

Strength for battles never comes up in Solomon's request. He asks for "…an understanding heart to judge Your people and to discern between good and evil." (1 Kings 3:9). His request is about judging and discerning. The job in front of him is leading a huge people.

The text doesn't say that. Solomon never mentions people refusing to obey him. His reason is a question: "For who is able to govern this great people of Yours?" (1 Kings 3:9). He's looking at the size of the job, not at anyone's attitude.

Right, it's false. Solomon doesn't say anyone refuses to obey. He asks, "For who is able to govern this great people of Yours?" (1 Kings 3:9). His need comes from the size of the people and the weight of the job. That's all the text gives.
Yes. God says, "…I will do what you have asked." (1 Kings 3:12). The text says it pleased the Lord that Solomon made this request (1 Kings 3:10). The answer is a plain yes. No fine print, friend.

The text says the opposite. God tells Solomon, "…I will do what you have asked." (1 Kings 3:12). It had already pleased the Lord that Solomon made this request (1 Kings 3:10). So God says yes to what Solomon asked.
That's the word. God says, "I will give you a wise and discerning heart…" (1 Kings 3:12). Wise and discerning, the very thing Solomon asked for. It's a gift to Solomon, the king, and it's a big one.
Brave is a good quality, but it's not the word God uses. He says, "I will give you a wise and discerning heart…" (1 Kings 3:12). The blank is wise. That matches Solomon's request for understanding.

Gentle, friend? That's a lovely word, but God picks a different one. In the dream He says, "I will give you a wise and discerning heart…" (1 Kings 3:12). Wise is the blank, and it fits what Solomon asked for in verse 9: an understanding heart.

The text says the opposite. God says, "…so that there will never have been another like you, nor will there ever be." (1 Kings 3:12). That means none before him and none after him. So no, nobody like him is coming someday.
Right. God says, "…so that there will never have been another like you, nor will there ever be." (1 Kings 3:12). Nobody before, nobody after. That is some serious wisdom, friend.

Yes! God says, "Moreover, I will give you what you did not request—both riches and honor…" (1 Kings 3:13). Solomon asked for wisdom, and God promises riches and honor too. I think that's the best kind of surprise.

Strength and speed aren't in God's list here. He says, "Moreover, I will give you what you did not request—both riches and honor…" (1 Kings 3:13). The extras are riches and honor. Nobody's racing anybody in this verse, friend.

Those aren't the words God uses for the extras. He says, "Moreover, I will give you what you did not request—both riches and honor…" (1 Kings 3:13). A promise about his days does come a verse later, and it has an "if" attached (1 Kings 3:14). The thing Solomon didn't request here is riches and honor.

That's the word. God says, "So if you walk in My ways and keep My statutes and commandments, just as your father David did, I will prolong your days." (1 Kings 3:14). Notice the "if." The promise is tied to walking in God's ways, the way David did.

Brighten sounds pleasant, but God doesn't say it. He says, "…I will prolong your days." (1 Kings 3:14). The word is prolong, and it comes after an "if" about walking in His ways and keeping His statutes and commandments.

Fill is a fine word, but it isn't the one in the verse. God says, "…I will prolong your days." (1 Kings 3:14). Prolong is the word, and it follows an "if" about walking in His ways and keeping His statutes and commandments, just as David did.

explanations.answer: He holds a feast for them
explanations.explanation: That's right. After the offerings, the text says, "Then he held a feast for all his servants." (1 Kings 3:15). Solomon wakes from the dream, goes before the ark, and then throws a feast. I'd show up early for that one, friend.

explanations.answer: He gives each one a gift
explanations.explanation: Gifts aren't mentioned here. The text says, "Then he held a feast for all his servants." (1 Kings 3:15). The servants get a feast, and nothing about presents. Sounds like a good party, though.

explanations.answer: He frees every one of them
explanations.explanation: Freeing every servant? Nice thought, friend, but that's not in this passage. The text says, "Then he held a feast for all his servants." (1 Kings 3:15). The servants get a feast, and I'd be first in line with a fresh batch of cookies.
